title: Orion Analytics — POC unit econ & benchmark scoping

Orion to provide 48-hour representative request trace (by 2025-09-18)
Schedule 2-hour benchmark run with Orion's test VPC (w/c 2025-09-22)
action_items: Maya Chen: Share detailed cost model (spreadsheet) — due 2025-09-15
Luca Romano: Draft benchmark plan & metrics (p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost-per-1k) — due 2025-09-17

summary: Discovery/POC scoping call focused on cost modeling for a proposed 6-week POC. Customer provided workload shape and budget constraints; Redwood outlined batching/caching levers, expected per-token estimates for different quantization and dedicated vs hosted options, and proposed benchmark plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Priya: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Marcus: Good morning, thanks for setting this up.
[00:09] Maya: Cool. Quick agenda: 1) understand your success criteria for the POC, 2) go through workload and current costs, 3) discuss benchmark plan and timelines, 4) next steps. Luca from engineering will walk through batching/caching knobs.
[00:25] Luca (SE): Hi all, quick intro — I focus on inference perf and cost. I'll try to keep the deep stuff tangible.
[00:34] Samir: We're mainly concerned about unit cost and predictable latency for our summarization pipeline.
[00:40] Priya: To add, we need to validate that switching to a dedicated inference layer doesn't blow our budget. We run on-prem for some sensitive data but okay to run hosted for anonymized workflows.
[00:52] Maya: Great. Marcus, can you run through current volume and token mix?
[00:57] Marcus: Sure. Baseline is ~120k requests/day NRT, avg prompt length ~220 tokens, avg response ~420 tokens, so roughly 640 tokens per request. Peak QPS around 35 at 9am PST, sustained 12–15 during business hours. We have a small subset of heavy jobs — about 2% of requests are 3k+ tokens.
[01:22] Priya: Our SLAs target 500ms p95 for interactive uses, but batch workflows can take longer.
[01:28] Elena: Network egress costs are non-trivial for us; we want to understand not just per-token but end-to-end cost including VPC peering.
[01:36] Luca: Totally makes sense. Quick math on your numbers — 120k * 640 tokens ≈ 76.8M tokens/day, about 2.3B tokens/month.
[01:48] Priya: That — yeah, that's high. Our current spend on hosted endpoints is roughly $28k/mo for inference and infra, so we're hoping to get to sub-$15k with a POC and optimizations.
[02:00] Maya: Understood. For scope, are you imagining a 4–6 week POC to prove unit economics and latency?
[02:07] Priya: 6 weeks preferred. Need a production-like ramp for at least two weeks.
[02:12] Marcus: We also need a go/no-go checklist: cost per 1k tokens below $0.80, p95 latency < 600ms for interactive routes, and correctness metrics (ROUGE / human checks) not regressing more than 3 points.
[02:28] Maya: Good, that's actionable. Luca — show knobs we can tune to hit that cost x latency target.
[02:34] Luca: Right. There are a few levers: model size and quantization (e.g., 8-bit vs 4-bit), batching policy (max batch size, dynamic batching window), KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts, and routing to cheaper model variants for low-fidelity tasks.
[02:51] Priya: When you say caching, do you mean prefix cache or full response cache? Most of our requests share similar context — the product description and user history.
[02:59] Luca: Both are possible. Prefix/K V cache helps because it reduces compute on the left context; full-response caching can return identical responses for exact inputs. We can evaluate hit rates from your trace. Even a 10–15% cache hit can materially reduce token compute.
[03:12] Marcus: Can you give ballpark per-token numbers for hosted vs dedicated and for quantized variants?
[03:17] Maya: Luca — do you want to throw some ranges? These are high-level — we'll do detailed spreadsheet later.
[03:22] Luca: Sure. Hosted (multi-tenant) with full-precision model: roughly $0.0008–0.0012 per token at current market dynamics for similar sized models. Dedicated GPU pools with 8-bit quantization: $0.00025–0.00045 per token. With 4-bit quant and aggressive caching/batching you can get toward $0.00015–0.0003 per token. Those are approximate; actual depends on batchability and sequence length distribution.
[03:50] Priya: So at 2.3B tokens/month, that delta is huge. If we hit $0.0003/token that's ~$690k/mo — wait that math seems off.
[03:59] Luca: Quick correction — 2.3B tokens * $0.0003 = $690k, yep — so we need to make sure numbers align. If you're at $28k/mo today, perhaps your currently billed tokens are lower or you're on different pricing model. Are you including embeddings and other costs?
[04:14] Marcus: Our current number was taking into account some pre-aggregation — maybe I mis-read. We'll send a sample billing export.
[04:20] Samir: Our target budget for the POC is $10k/month — meaning Redwood stack + infra should be within that for workload subset.
[04:28] Maya: That helps. For POC we can scope a representative slice — maybe 10% of production traffic — to validate unit economics. That would cut tokens to ~230M/mo for the POC, which at $0.0003/token becomes $69k — still above target.
[04:44] Priya: That's alarming. Can we talk about batching savings?
[04:47] Luca: Absolutely. Batching can reduce per-token GPU overhead. If you have high concurrency and similar seq lengths, effective cost per token can drop 20–50% depending on kernel efficiency. For example, moving from batch size 4 to batch 16 with continuous batching reduces per-token time and amortizes kernel launch. Also our smart routing can send low-priority traffic to cheaper variants.
[05:07] Marcus: What about latency trade-offs? If we batch more, p95 could spike.
[05:12] Luca: There's a window setting. Continuous batching uses a small micro-second window — you can bias toward latency or throughput. For interactive routes we'll keep window small to preserve p95. For async/batch jobs we can increase to maximize throughput.
[05:24] Elena: Any numbers on p95 change?
[05:27] Luca: Roughly, for interactive config we expect p95 to remain within 1.1–1.3x of single-request latency; if single-request is 200ms p95 then batched might be 220–260ms. For heavy batching throughput optimized lanes p95 for individual request might be higher but amortized cost drops.
[05:43] Priya: How do we measure and compare — what metrics do you suggest we collect during the benchmark?
[05:47] Maya: We typically collect tokens/sec, GPU utilization, p50/p95/p99 latency, cost-per-1k-tokens (billed), cache hit rate, and model quality delta on a fixed evaluation set. Luca will propose exact dashboard metrics.
[06:00] Luca: I'll include per-shard metrics and per-route breakdowns so you can see which routes are driving cost. Also will include trace sampling to show where KV cache helped.
[06:09] Marcus: About quantization — will it change output quality? Our legal/compliance team needs to validate hallucination risk.
[06:16] Luca: Good question. 8-bit generally has minimal quality regression for many models; 4-bit can introduce subtle differences. We'll run A/B evals on your prompt set and human spot checks. We expect <2–3% metric drift for 8-bit in most cases, but we'll validate.
[06:32] Priya: Timeline for the POC — you mentioned 6 weeks. Can you break down milestones?
[06:36] Maya: Week 0: data exchange and environment setup. Week 1: baseline run (no optimizations), Week 2–3: tuning (batching, caching, quant), Week 4: larger-scale ramp, Week 5: final benchmarks & quality evals, Week 6: review + decision. We can shift based on your readiness.
[06:55] Marcus: For environment — do you need VPC peering or can you run in hosted test harness?
[06:59] Elena: We prefer a test VPC with peering for privacy, though for anonymized subsets hosted is ok.
[07:05] Maya: We support both. For peered VPC tests we need a couple firewall rules and a test account; Luca will coordinate on specifics.
[07:12] Luca: Yes, I'll send the checklist. Also note we'll need a synthetic load generator to replay your trace; we can help with that.
[07:19] Priya: Ok. About the cost model spreadsheet — what inputs do you need from us?
[07:23] Luca: Sequence length distribution, per-route QPS profile, percentage of cacheable requests, acceptable p95 latency target per route, and any compliance-related egress constraints. If you can provide a 48-hour sample trace that includes timestamps and token counts that's ideal.
[07:38] Samir: We'll pull that — but curious: how conservative are your per-token estimates? Can you give a slightly more realistic example using our numbers at 10% sample?
[07:46] Luca: If we run a POC at 10% sample (230M tokens/mo): with dedicated 8-bit and modest caching (15% hit) and batching tuned for interactive + async split, realistic per-token might be $0.00045 — that comes to ~$103k/mo scaled to full prod. For JUST the POC subset that'd be around $103k * 0.1 = $10.3k — which is close to your POC budget target. The key is hit rate and batchability.
[08:14] Priya: That actually sounds promising — hitting POC budget if we scope properly.
[08:17] Marcus: We need to understand non-GPU infra billed by cloud — will Redwood show an itemized cost breakdown?
[08:23] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console breaks down token-level compute, GPU hours, egress, and storage. We'll include that in the spreadsheet so you can map to your cloud bill.
[08:33] Elena: About compliance: SOC2 and audit logs are mandatory for us. We may need a scan of retention policies and KMS integration for Private.
[08:42] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II docs and a Private deployment option with K M S/HSM integration. I'll attach our security pack.
[08:50] Priya: Good. Another question: do you support canary / fallback policies? We want graceful degradation to smaller models if capacity is constrained.
[08:58] Luca: Yes, smart routing can fallback to smaller variants and we can set cost-vs-latency policies. For POC we can simulate failure/fallback to observe user impact.
[09:06] Samir: Let's talk about benchmarks: how long will a benchmark run need to be to be meaningful?
[09:10] Luca: For stability we recommend a 2–4 hour run at sustained QPS for each config, plus a 24–48h ramp to catch diurnal patterns. For perf counters like p99 you want at least ~10k samples.
[09:21] Maya: Proposed benchmark plan in brief: baseline run (2h), optimization run (2h) for each major config (8-bit, 4-bit, routing), and a 48h long-run for production-like ramp. Luca will finalize exact schedule.
[09:36] Marcus: If results look good, what's the next step commercially?
[09:39] Maya: Typically after favorable benchmarks we move to a pilot contract for Dedicated capacity — monthly reserved — with an initial commitment sized to your peak needs, plus a short-term discount for the POC. Pricing & terms to be shared after the benchmark.
[09:53] Priya: Any other hidden costs we should consider?
[09:56] Luca: Watch out for unusually long sequences (3k+ tokens) which can spike memory and kernel selection costs; cold KV cache miss storms during ramp; and egress. We'll flag those in the runbook.
[10:08] Elena: For the POC we'll also want a synthetic failure test — do you support chaos tests?
[10:12] Luca: Yes, we can simulate node loss and see failover to other pools. We'll include that in week 5.
[10:18] Maya: Great. To wrap, I'll repeat next steps: Maya sends cost model spreadsheet + security pack; Luca sends benchmark plan and VPC checklist; Orion provides 48h trace and confirms test VPC access.
[10:30] Priya: Sounds good.
[10:32] Marcus: One last nit — for the per-token math in the spreadsheet please include an "effective token" column that accounts for caching (so we can see raw tokens vs billed compute tokens).
[10:42] Luca: Will do. We'll also include a sensitivity table (cache hit 0–30%, batch sizes 1–32).
[10:49] Samir: Thanks — this was productive.
[10:51] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with dates.
[10:55] Priya: Bye all.
[10:56] Marcus: Thanks.
[10:58] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: automated transcript contains a few mis-typed acronyms (K V cache rendered as K V, VPC as V P C) and occasional filler words. References shared: cost-model-template.xlsx (link sent in chat), redwood-security-pack.pdf (link).
